[[Columbia Records|Columbia]] (US) | writer = [[Paul McCartney]] | producer = [[George Martin]] | chronology = [[Paul McCartney]] | prev_title = [[Temporary Secretary]] | prev_year = 1980 | next_title = [[Take It Away (Paul McCartney song)|Take It Away]] | next_year = 1982 | misc = {{Extra chronology | artist = [[Stevie Wonder]] | type = single | prev_title = [[Do I Do]] | prev_year = 1982 | title = Ebony and Ivory | year = 1982 | next_title = [[Ribbon in the Sky]] | next_year = 1982 }} {{External music video|header=Official video| {{YouTube|fXAlfh6QKQs|"Ebony and Ivory"}}}} }} "'''Ebony and Ivory'''" is a song that was released in 1982 as a [[single (music)|single]] by [[Paul McCartney]] featuring [[Stevie Wonder]]. It was issued on 29 March that year as the lead single from McCartney's third solo album, ''[[Tug of War (Paul McCartney album)|Tug of War]]'' (1982). Written by McCartney, the song aligns the black and white keys of a piano keyboard with the theme of racial harmony. The single reached number one on both the UK and the US charts and was among the top-selling singles of 1982 in the US. During the [[apartheid]] era, the [[South African Broadcasting Corporation]] banned the song after Wonder dedicated his 1984 [[Academy Award for Best Original Song]] (for "[[I Just Called to Say I Love You]]") to [[Nelson Mandela]]. McCartney and Wonder began recording "Ebony and Ivory" in Montserrat in early 1981. The single marked the first time that McCartney had released a duet with another major artist and anticipated his 1980s collaborations with [[Michael Jackson]]. The track also appears on McCartney compilations ''[[All the Best!]]'' (1987) and ''[[Pure McCartney (Paul McCartney album)|Pure McCartney]]'' (2016), and on the two-disc version of Wonder's ''[[The Definitive Collection (Stevie Wonder album)#UK|The Definitive Collection]]'' (2002). In 2013, ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' ranked it as the 69th-biggest hit of all-time on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] charts.{{cite magazine|url= http://www.billboard.com/articles/list/2155531/the-hot-100-all-time-top-songs?list_page=3 |title= Hot 100 55th Anniversary: The All-Time Top 100 Songs |magazine= Billboard |date= 2 August 2012 |access-date= 9 August 2013 |first= Fred |last= Bronson}}

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
McCartney wrote "Ebony and Ivory" at his farm in Scotland in 1978.<ref name="M&E p 266">{{cite book|last1=Madinger|first1=Chip|last2=Easter|first2=Mark|title=Eight Arms to Hold You: The Solo Beatles Compendium|publisher=44.1 Productions|location=Chesterfield, MO|year=2000|isbn=0-615-11724-4|page=266}}</ref> He first rehearsed the song with [[Paul McCartney and Wings|Wings]] in 1979.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kozinn |first1=Allan |last2=Sinclair |first2=Adrian |title=The McCartney Legacy: Volume 2: 1974–80 |date=10 December 2024 |publisher=HarperCollins |isbn=978-0-06-300077-3 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nQf7EAAAQBAJ |access-date=11 May 2025 |language=en}}</ref> The song uses the [[ebony]] (black) and [[ivory]] (white) keys on a [[piano]] as a metaphor for [[Racial integration|integration]] and racial harmony. The title was inspired by McCartney hearing [[Spike Milligan]] say, "Black notes, white notes, and you need to play the two to make harmony, folks!"<ref>Martin, George (editor): ''Making Music'', page 62. Pan Books, 1983. {{ISBN|0-330-26945-3}}</ref> The [[figure of speech]] is much older. It was popularised by [[James Aggrey]] in the 1920s, inspiring the title of the pan-African journal ''[[The Keys (journal)|The Keys]]'', but was in use from at least the 1840s.<ref>'Master and mistress, and neighbors, and negroes assemble, and black and white are seen strung along the great table, like the keys of a piano, and, like the aforesaid instrument, the black keys make fully as much noise as the white; all mingle for a while in the utmost harmony and good feeling ...' Rev C F Sturgis, 'Duties of Christian Masters to their Slaves' (1849) quoted in Breedon, James O (editor), ''Advice among Masters: The Ideal in Slave Management in the Old South'' (Westport, CT: Greenwood Press, 1980), page 262.</ref>

While writing the song, McCartney envisaged singing it with a black male singer.<ref name="M&E p 266" /> He and Wonder recorded it together at [[George Martin]]'s [[AIR Montserrat|AIR Studios]] in [[Montserrat]]<ref>{{cite book|last=Sounes|first=Howard|author-link=Howard Sounes|title=Fab: An Intimate Life of Paul McCartney|publisher=HarperCollins|location=London|year=2010|isbn=978-0-00-723705-0|pages=372–73}}</ref> during sessions lasting from 27 February to 2 March 1981. McCartney then carried out overdubs on the track at AIR in London.{{sfn|Madinger|Easter|2000|p=263}} Due to conflicting work schedules, McCartney and Wonder filmed their parts for the song's music video separately (as explained by McCartney in his commentary for ''[[The McCartney Years]]'' 3-DVD boxed set).

A video for the solo version was also made, which showed McCartney playing piano with a bright spotlight, and black men in prison, including one of them being uplifted by the song, dancing and listening to it in prison as well as in the studio. This version was directed by Barry Myers on 11 February 1982. That same day, McCartney filmed a promotional interview for the ''Tug of War'' album.<ref name="M&E p 266"/>

The [[B-side]] of the single, "Rainclouds", was written by McCartney and [[Denny Laine]], though on early pressings of the single the song was credited only to McCartney.<ref name="jpgr">{{cite web|url=http://www.jpgr.co.uk/r6054.html|title=Ebony and Ivory |year=2000 |publisher=JPGR |access-date=2013-09-25}}</ref> According to authors Chip Madinger and Mark Easter, "Rainclouds" is "perhaps most notorious" as the track that McCartney worked on during 9 December 1980, straight after hearing that [[John Lennon]] had been [[Murder of John Lennon|fatally shot in New York]].{{sfn|Madinger|Easter|2000|pp=263, 267}} When leaving AIR Studios in central London that evening, he said in response to a TV reporter's question about the murder: "drag, isn't it?"{{sfn|Madinger|Easter|2000|p=263}} The footage was included in news broadcasts around the world and McCartney's apparent casualness, though masking his profound shock, earned condemnation from the press.{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=369}}<ref>{{cite book|last=Rodriguez|first=Robert|title=Fab Four FAQ 2.0: The Beatles' Solo Years, 1970–1980|publisher=Backbeat Books|location=Milwaukee, WI|year=2010|isbn=978-1-4165-9093-4|pages=455–56|url=https://archive.org/details/missodellmyhardd00odel}}</ref>
sections.text:
McCartney wrote "Ebony and Ivory" at his farm in Scotland in 1978. He first rehearsed the song with Wings in 1979. The song uses the ebony (black) and ivory (white) keys on a piano as a metaphor for integration and racial harmony. The title was inspired by McCartney hearing Spike Milligan say, "Black notes, white notes, and you need to play the two to make harmony, folks!" The figure of speech is much older. It was popularised by James Aggrey in the 1920s, inspiring the title of the pan-African journal The Keys, but was in use from at least the 1840s.

While writing the song, McCartney envisaged singing it with a black male singer. He and Wonder recorded it together at George Martin's AIR Studios in Montserrat during sessions lasting from 27 February to 2 March 1981. McCartney then carried out overdubs on the track at AIR in London.{{sfn|Madinger|Easter|2000|p=263}} Due to conflicting work schedules, McCartney and Wonder filmed their parts for the song's music video separately (as explained by McCartney in his commentary for The McCartney Years 3-DVD boxed set).

A video for the solo version was also made, which showed McCartney playing piano with a bright spotlight, and black men in prison, including one of them being uplifted by the song, dancing and listening to it in prison as well as in the studio. This version was directed by Barry Myers on 11 February 1982. That same day, McCartney filmed a promotional interview for the Tug of War album.

The B-side of the single, "Rainclouds", was written by McCartney and Denny Laine, though on early pressings of the single the song was credited only to McCartney. According to authors Chip Madinger and Mark Easter, "Rainclouds" is "perhaps most notorious" as the track that McCartney worked on during 9 December 1980, straight after hearing that John Lennon had been fatally shot in New York.{{sfn|Madinger|Easter|2000|pp=263, 267}} When leaving AIR Studios in central London that evening, he said in response to a TV reporter's question about the murder: "drag, isn't it?"{{sfn|Madinger|Easter|2000|p=263}} The footage was included in news broadcasts around the world and McCartney's apparent casualness, though masking his profound shock, earned condemnation from the press.{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=369}}

sections.heading: Release and chart performance
sections.wikitext:
The "Ebony and Ivory" single was released on 29 March 1982 in both the UK and the United States.{{sfn|Madinger|Easter|2000|pp=590, 594}} It marked the first time in McCartney's solo career that he had sung a [[duet]] with another major star. In this, McCartney and Wonder fitted a trend as duetting artists became commonplace throughout the 1980s, particularly in mainstream British pop.<ref>{{cite book|last=Clayson|first=Alan|author-link=Alan Clayson|title=Paul McCartney|year=2003|publisher=Sanctuary|location=London|isbn=1-86074-482-6|pages=205–06}}</ref>

The single spent seven weeks at number one on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in the US{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=380}} and it was the fourth-biggest hit there of 1982.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20061020154415/http://www.billboard.com/bbcom/charts/yearend_chart_display.jsp?f=The+Billboard+Hot+100&g=Year-end+Singles&year=1982 ''Billboard'' Year-End Hot 100 Singles – 1982]</ref> Its commercial success was aided by the music video, with [[MTV]] having been launched the year before.{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=380}} The song was also number one in the UK and spent three weeks atop the [[Irish Singles Chart]].{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=380}}<ref>{{cite web|title=Official Charts: Paul McCartney|url=http://www.theofficialcharts.com/artist/_/paul%20mccartney/|publisher=The Official UK Charts Company|access-date=2011-10-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Irish Charts - All there is to know |url=https://www.irma.ie/search/%2A |access-date=2023-07-06 |website=www.irishcharts.ie}}</ref>

In the US, the single's run atop the chart was the longest of any of McCartney's post-[[Beatles]] works, and the second longest career-wise (behind the Beatles' "[[Hey Jude]]"). For Wonder, it was his longest-running chart-topper and made him the first solo artist to achieve a number-one single in the US over three consecutive decades.<ref>Whitburn, Joel, "Top Pop Singles: 1955–2006", 2007.</ref> It marked the first time that any single released by any member of the Beatles placed on the ''Billboard'' R&B chart. It was McCartney's record 28th song to hit number one on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100.<ref>{{Cite episode |title=American Top 40 replay |location=Green Bay, Wisconsin |date=1982-05-22 }}</ref>

In 2008, "Ebony and Ivory" was ranked at number 59 on ''Billboard''{{'}}s Hot 100 songs of all-time.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://www.billboard.com/bbcom/specials/hot100/charts/top100-titles-60.shtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080913210012/http://www.billboard.com/bbcom/specials/hot100/charts/top100-titles-60.shtml |url-status=dead |archive-date=13 September 2008 |title=The ''Billboard'' Hot 100 All-Time Top Songs (60–51) |magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |access-date=2009-08-30}}</ref> It was ranked 69th on a similar list published by the magazine in 2013.<ref name="Bronson 3"/>

In this, McCartney and Wonder fitted a trend as duetting artists became commonplace throughout the 1980s, particularly in mainstream British pop.

The single spent seven weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in the US{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=380}} and it was the fourth-biggest hit there of 1982. Its commercial success was aided by the music video, with MTV having been launched the year before.{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=380}} The song was also number one in the UK and spent three weeks atop the Irish Singles Chart.{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=380}}

In the US, the single's run atop the chart was the longest of any of McCartney's post-Beatles works, and the second longest career-wise (behind the Beatles' "Hey Jude"). For Wonder, it was his longest-running chart-topper and made him the first solo artist to achieve a number-one single in the US over three consecutive decades. It marked the first time that any single released by any member of the Beatles placed on the Billboard R&B chart. It was McCartney's record 28th song to hit number one on the Billboard Hot 100.

In 2008, "Ebony and Ivory" was ranked at number 59 on Billboard{{'}}s Hot 100 songs of all-time. It was ranked 69th on a similar list published by the magazine in 2013.

sections.heading: Critical reception and legacy
sections.wikitext:
''[[Record World]]'' said it has "a pretty pop melody and sing-along chorus [[hook (music)|hook]]."<ref name=rw>{{cite magazine|magazine=Record World|date=April 10, 1982|page=1|accessdate=2023-03-02|title=Hits of the Week|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/80s/82/Record-World-1982-04-10.pdf}}</ref>

Some critics have derided the song as "[[sentimentality|saccharine]]".<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CxGme_8G2MsC&q=saccharine+ebony+and+ivory&pg=PA281|title=Still the Greatest: The Essential Songs of the Beatles' Solo Careers|first=Andrew Grant|last=Jackson|year=2012|publisher=Scarecrow Press|access-date=3 March 2017|via=Google Books|isbn=9780810882225}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/music/music-news/9038679/Sir-Paul-McCartney-and-Stevie-Wonder-back-in-the-studio-together-for-the-first-time-30-years.html|title=Sir Paul McCartney and Stevie Wonder back in the studio together for the first time 30 years|newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|date=25 January 2012|access-date=3 March 2017|last1=Alleyne|first1=Richard}}</ref> According to Madinger and Easter, the most common reaction 20 years later was that it marked "the beginning of the end of [McCartney's] artistic credibility". They add that while the song appealed to listeners who would never usually have bought a McCartney record, it "wore out its welcome quickly" and came to be seen as him attempting to stay musically relevant in middle age, particularly as he soon went on to record duets with [[Michael Jackson]].<ref name="M&E p 266" />

In 2007, [[BBC 6 Music]] listeners voted "Ebony and Ivory" the worst duet in history.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/entertainment/7031695.stm |title=Ebony and Ivory voted worst duet |date=2007-10-06 |access-date=2007-10-08 |work=BBC News}}</ref> Two years later, ''[[Blender magazine|Blender]]'' magazine named it as the tenth-[[List of music considered the worst|worst song of all time]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.blender.com/lists/61412/the50worstsongseverwatchlistenandcringe.html?p=9 |title=Run for Your Life! It's the 50 Worst Songs Ever! |work=[[Blender magazine|Blender]] |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091231160555/http://www.blender.com/lists/61412/the50worstsongseverwatchlistenandcringe.html?p=9 |archive-date=31 December 2009 }}</ref> Writing in 2010, biographer [[Howard Sounes]] said that while many people consider the song to be "annoyingly simplistic", it contains "the ineluctable power of McCartney's best tunes" and was a "massive hit".{{sfn|Sounes|2010|p=373}}

"Ebony and Ivory" was banned in South Africa by the [[South African Broadcasting Corporation]] during the [[apartheid]] era, making it the only song McCartney released in his solo career to receive such a ban. The official reason for the ban was because Wonder accepted his 1984 [[Academy Award for Best Original Song]] "in the name of [[Nelson Mandela]]".<ref name=wonder>{{cite news |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9F00E4DD1438F934A15750C0A963948260 |title=Stevie Wonder Music Banned in South Africa |date=27 March 1985 |work=The New York Times |access-date=26 May 2008 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/inatl/longterm/s_africa/stories/star072598.htm |title=Mandela: South Africa's Star Attractor |date=1998-07-25 |access-date=2012-02-11 |newspaper=The Washington Post}}</ref>

Part of a phrase from the song's lyrics provided the title for ''[[Keyboard, Oh Lord! Why Don't We?]]'', a 2005 album by the Norwegian [[stoner rock]] band [[Thulsa Doom (band)|Thulsa Doom]].

sections.heading: Screen depictions
sections.wikitext:
The song and video were spoofed in a 1982 ''[[Saturday Night Live]]'' sketch, with [[Eddie Murphy]] portraying Wonder and [[Joe Piscopo]], as [[Frank Sinatra]], assuming McCartney's role. In the sketch, Sinatra criticises the "ebony and ivory" metaphor for racial equality (which was deemed by many critics to be overly simplistic, to the point of being insulting) as being "too artsy for the public – capisce?" After a brief exchange, the duo perform the song with more direct, and offensive, lyrics ("You are black, and I am white / Life's an Eskimo Pie, let's take a bite!").<ref>{{cite web |url=https://snltranscripts.jt.org/81/81tebonyivory.phtml |title=SNL Transcripts Tonight: Ebony & Ivory |date=2018-10-08 |access-date=2019-10-17 |publisher=SNL Transcripts Tonight}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Frank Sinatra and Stevie Wonder Duet - SNL | date=13 July 2019 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0h2jZtuRuic |access-date=2023-03-31 |language=en}}</ref>

The song and video were parodied in a commercial for the 2008 season of the [[USA Network]] show ''[[Psych]]''.<ref>{{YouTube|ZvM3RHLyzOo|PSYCH Sing-Along "Ebony & Ivory"}}</ref> The ''[[South Park]]'' [[South Park (season 25)|season 25]] episode "[[The Big Fix (South Park)|The Big Fix]]" (2022) features a parody of the song called "Black Puppy, White Puppy". Dan Caffrey of ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' suggests that McCartney may have denied a request from producers [[Trey Parker]] and [[Matt Stone]] for the song's inclusion in the episode, thus necessitating the parody.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.avclub.com/south-park-recap-season-25-episode-2-1848512624 |title=South Park heads back to Middle-earth to lampoon performative allyship |date=2022-02-09 |access-date=2022-02-10 |work=AV Club}}</ref>
sections.text:
The song and video were spoofed in a 1982 Saturday Night Live sketch, with Eddie Murphy portraying Wonder and Joe Piscopo, as Frank Sinatra, assuming McCartney's role. In the sketch, Sinatra criticises the "ebony and ivory" metaphor for racial equality (which was deemed by many critics to be overly simplistic, to the point of being insulting) as being "too artsy for the public – capisce?" After a brief exchange, the duo perform the song with more direct, and offensive, lyrics ("You are black, and I am white / Life's an Eskimo Pie, let's take a bite!").

The song and video were parodied in a commercial for the 2008 season of the USA Network show Psych. The South Park season 25 episode "The Big Fix" (2022) features a parody of the song called "Black Puppy, White Puppy". Dan Caffrey of The A.V. Club suggests that McCartney may have denied a request from producers Trey Parker and Matt Stone for the song's inclusion in the episode, thus necessitating the parody.
